questions.stem: Which four groups are bonded to the central carbon of an amino acid?

options.text: An amine group, a carboxyl group, a hydrogen atom and an R group
options.why: Every amino acid has the same first three. Only the R group changes from one amino acid to the next.

options.text: An amine group, a phosphate group, a hydrogen atom and an R group
options.why: Phosphate groups belong in nucleotides and phospholipids. An amino acid has a carboxyl group there.

options.text: A hydroxyl group, a carboxyl group, a hydrogen atom and an R group
options.why: The "amino" in amino acid is the amine group. A hydroxyl group isn't one of the four.

options.text: An amine group, a carboxyl group, a methyl group and a peptide bond
options.why: A peptide bond only forms when two amino acids join, and the fourth group is a hydrogen atom.

questions.stem: What happens when two amino acids join by condensation?

options.text: A water molecule is used up to split them apart
options.why: That's hydrolysis, the reverse reaction. Condensation releases water.

options.text: A peptide bond forms and water is released
options.why: The amine group of one reacts with the carboxyl group of the other. You get a dipeptide and one molecule of water.

options.text: A hydrogen bond forms between their R groups
options.why: The link between amino acids in a chain is a peptide bond, which is covalent. R groups aren't involved.

options.text: A disulfide bond forms and CO2 is released
options.why: Disulfide bonds form between two cysteines in tertiary structure. They don't join amino acids into a chain.

questions.stem: A polypeptide is 150 amino acids long. How many water molecules were released when it was made?

options.why: Count the bonds, not the amino acids. A chain of 150 has one fewer bond than it has amino acids.
One water comes off for each peptide bond, and a chain of 150 amino acids has 149 bonds.
There's one bond fewer than the number of amino acids, not one more.
Each condensation releases one water, not two.

options.text: It's needed in larger amounts than the others
options.why: "Essential" isn't about amount or importance. It's about where the amino acid has to come from.

options.text: It's found in every protein the body makes
options.why: Plenty of proteins lack particular amino acids. That isn't what the word means here.

options.text: The body can't make it, so it must come from food
options.why: Non-essential ones can be made from other compounds. Essential ones can't, so a diet short of one limits protein synthesis.

options.text: It's the only type that can form peptide bonds
options.why: Every amino acid can form peptide bonds. Essential describes diet, not chemistry.

questions.stem: How many different sequences are possible for a peptide three amino acids long?

options.why: That's 20 × 3. Each of the three positions multiplies the choices, so it's 20 × 20 × 20.
That's 20 squared, which is the answer for two amino acids, not three.
That counts combinations where order doesn't matter. In a peptide order matters, so it's 20 to the power of 3.
Any of 20 amino acids can go in each position, so it's 20 to the power of 3.

questions.stem: An enzyme is heated until it denatures. Which bonds are still intact?

options.text: Hydrogen bonds holding the secondary structure
options.why: Those are among the first to break when a protein is heated.

options.text: Ionic bonds between charged R groups
options.why: Ionic bonds in the tertiary structure are disrupted by denaturation. That's part of why the shape changes.

options.text: Peptide bonds between the amino acids
options.why: Denaturation changes the shape, not the sequence. The chain is still one piece afterward.

options.text: Hydrophobic interactions in the interior
options.why: Heat disrupts those too, which is part of why the protein unfolds.

questions.stem: Which statement about denaturation is correct?

options.text: It's always permanent once the shape is lost
options.why: Mild denaturation can reverse. Writing "always permanent" loses the mark.

options.text: It can be reversible or irreversible, depending on severity
options.why: Some proteins refold when normal conditions return. Severe heat or extreme pH can make the change permanent.

options.text: It breaks the protein back down into amino acids
options.why: That would be hydrolysis. Denaturation leaves the chain of amino acids whole.

options.text: It only happens at temperatures above 100 °C
options.why: Many proteins denature well below boiling, and pH changes can denature them at any temperature.

questions.stem: How does a change in pH denature a protein?

options.text: It changes the charges on R groups, disrupting ionic bonds
options.why: Adding or removing H+ changes which R groups are charged, so ionic and hydrogen bonds holding the shape break.

options.text: It hydrolyzes the peptide bonds along the backbone
options.why: pH changes disrupt the folding, not the peptide bonds. The sequence stays the same.

options.text: It adds extra amino acids to the end of the chain
options.why: pH can't add amino acids. Only translation builds the chain.

options.text: It removes water from inside the folded protein
options.why: Losing water isn't the mechanism. pH works by changing the charges on R groups.

questions.stem: Which bonds hold a protein's secondary structure together?

options.text: Ionic bonds between oppositely charged R groups
options.why: That's tertiary structure. R-group bonds shape the whole chain, not the helix.

options.text: Disulfide bonds between pairs of cysteine R groups
options.why: Disulfide bonds are also R-group interactions, so they belong to tertiary structure.

options.text: Hydrogen bonds between backbone amine and carboxyl groups
options.why: The alpha helix and beta pleated sheet are the backbone folding on itself, so the R groups aren't involved yet.

options.text: Hydrophobic interactions between non-polar R groups
options.why: Those help fold the whole chain in tertiary structure, not the helix or sheet.

questions.stem: Which interactions hold a protein's tertiary structure together?

options.text: Peptide bonds only, between neighboring amino acids along the chain
options.why: Peptide bonds make the primary structure. The tertiary shape is held by R groups interacting.

options.text: Hydrogen, ionic and disulfide bonds plus hydrophobic interactions between R groups
options.why: Name all four and say they're between R groups. Listing "bonds" without naming them doesn't score.

options.text: Hydrogen bonds between backbone amine and carboxyl groups, and nothing else
options.why: That's secondary structure. Tertiary structure comes from the R groups.

options.text: Bonds between two or more separate polypeptide chains in one protein
options.why: That's quaternary structure. Tertiary is the shape of one chain.

questions.stem: Which protein is an example of quaternary structure?

options.text: Haemoglobin, made of four polypeptide chains
options.why: Quaternary structure means two or more polypeptides in one protein. Haemoglobin also has haem groups, so it's conjugated too.

options.text: Any enzyme, since every protein has four levels
options.why: Not every protein has quaternary structure. Many are a single polypeptide.

options.text: A single polypeptide folded into an alpha helix
options.why: One chain can't have quaternary structure, and a helix is secondary structure.

options.text: Any dipeptide formed from two amino acids
options.why: A dipeptide is two amino acids in one chain. Quaternary structure needs two or more chains.

questions.stem: Which description fits a globular protein?

options.text: Long and narrow, insoluble, with a structural role
options.why: That describes fibrous proteins like collagen and keratin.

options.text: Rounded and soluble, with a functional role
options.why: Enzymes, haemoglobin and insulin all fit. Their shape lets them do a job, not hold something up.

options.text: Repetitive in sequence, forming strong fibers
options.why: Repetitive sequences are a fibrous-protein feature. Globular proteins have irregular sequences.

options.text: Always embedded in the phospholipid bilayer
options.why: Some membrane proteins are globular, but most globular proteins, like enzymes, work in solution.
